newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's new rulers tighten grip on Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's new rulers tighten grip on Kabul.

text.p: Afghanistan's new hardline Islamist rulers tightened their grip on Kabul on Thursday, stopping residents from leaving as hundreds jammed the city's main bus station in an attempt to go towards neighbouring Pakistan.

"The people of Kabul are requested not to leave the city. Those who have left already may return and their security will be assured," said Mullah Mohammad Omar, leader and founder of the country's new Taleban militia regime.

Omar, in a decree published in the movement's newspaper Shariat, also renewed calls for the world to recognise the new administration and withdraw accreditation from all former government diplomatic missions.
"All ambassadors to foreign countries are suspended and have no authority to work," said Omar, who is based in the southern city of Kandahar.
"Different countries of the world are duty-bound to protect Afghanistan's properties abroad and no ambassador has the right to cash cheques," he said.

Witnesses said hundreds of people had been crowding the capital's main bus station at Pul-i-Mahmood Khan in the past few days, heading down the highway to the eastern city of Jalalabad en route to Pakistan.
At dawn on Thursday, Taleban fighters were stopping some Kabul residents from leaving with their household goods and families, the witnesses said.

The Taleban, seeking to enforce their strict version of Islamic sharia law, have ordered women government employees to stay at home, promising them full pay until workplaces can be reorganised to separate men and woman. Many woman in Kabul believe they will never be allowed to return to their jobs with the exception of those in the health sector.
"We are hoping the Taleban will keep their promise to pay us but we are not sure they will," said a newly-unemployed female teacher, who asked not to be named.
Omar asked mine clearance teams, many of them funded by the United Nations, to resume work especially on roads leading from Kabul, and said traders should bring food supplies into the city.
Kabul radio exhorted people to pray five times a day at their local mosque but did not say what would happen to those who failed to conform.

The Taleban movement, which seized the Afghan capital from the relatively moderate Islamic government of former President Burhanuddin Rabbani a week ago, has stamped its seal on the city with edicts reflecting its purist vision of Islamic behaviour.
In the process it has aroused growing international condemnation over its human rights performance and treatment of wowen.
The Taleban's military drive to extend its control over Afghanistan has provoked alarm among its northern neighbours.
The Commonwealth of Independent States plans to hold a summit starting in the Kazakh capital of Almaty on Friday to discuss the Taleban's stunning rise to power.
Russia's national security supremo, Alexander Lebed, said this week that the Taleban posed a threat to Moscow and the borders of Central Asian republics.

"If the Taleban, backed by Pakistan, reaches the borders with Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, including the city of Bokhara, they want to annex, they will wipe away Russian border posts and see the road to the north free," Lebed said.

The Taleban's most direct route to the north is blocked by the forces of ethnic Uzbek leader and former communist general Abdul Rashid Dostum, deployed in strength at the strategic Soviet-built Salang Tunnel through the towering Hindu Kush mountains, about 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul.
U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl visited Dostum in his hometown of Shibargan and Taleban leaders in Kabul on Wednesday in an attempt to avert a showdown.
Sources close to Dostum say he does not want to fight the Taleban but wants to keep them out of the six northern provinces he controls.

The Taleban, whose priority is to clear the Panjsher Valley northeast of Kabul or pro-Rabbani forces led by former government military chief Ahmad Shad Masood, say they have no quarrel with Dostum at the moment.
